paper.title: Interpolating between volume and lattice point enumerator with successive minima
paper.affiliation: Technische Universitaet Berlin; Universidad de Murcia
paper.source_of_truth: Mathematics cataloged from the authors' LaTeX e-print (arxiv.org/e-print/2105.13090v2, single file main.tex, 1291 lines after comment stripping). Every printed number, page and section reference is taken from the published open-access version of record (Springer, CC BY 4.0, 24 pages), because the two do not agree: the source numbers every display environment while the version of record leaves several unnumbered, so from Davenport's inequality onward a source-order number runs three ahead of the printed one. The version of record prints exactly 27 numbered equations: (1.1) to (1.16), (2.1), (4.1) to (4.5) and (5.1) to (5.5); section 3 prints none.
paper.scope_note: This is a theorem paper, not a framework paper. It proves two-sided bounds on the ratio between the lattice point enumerator G(K) and the volume of an n-dimensional convex body in terms of its successive minima (Theorem 1.1), deduces a bound of the shape G(K) <= prod (2/lambda_i + c_i) with c_i independent of the body (Corollary 1.2), reverses the Henze/Schymura projection inequality (Theorem 1.3), proves the conjectured planar upper bound and a weaker planar lower bound (Theorem 1.4), confirms the exact symmetric lower conjecture for origin-symmetric lattice polygons (Proposition 1.5), and gives tight covering-radius bounds (Proposition 1.6). The engine is a rearrangement: Blaschke's shaking reduces an arbitrary convex body to an anti-blocking one without changing the volume, without losing lattice points and without increasing any successive minimum (Theorem 3.1). Two conjectures of Betke, Henk and Wills are stated and not proved; later results establish only specified special cases or weakenings. The paper also quotes established results from other work, including Minkowski's second theorem, the Betke-Henk-Wills and Malikiosis bounds, Davenport's and Henze's projection inequalities, van der Corput's theorem, the Rogers-Shephard section-projection inequality, the covering-radius bound of Kannan and Lovasz, Pick's theorem, and the boundary bound of Henk, Schuermann and Wills. Each is cataloged separately from the paper's own results.

background_notation.|x|_K: the gauge or Minkowski functional of K

hypotheses: K is in K^n with K = -K.
items.statement_informal: The gauge of x is the least dilation factor needed for the dilated body to contain x.
items.statement_formal: |x|_K = inf { r > 0 : x in rK }; for x nonzero this infimum is the minimum printed by the paper, and |0|_K = 0.

items.formalization_notes: Use Mathlib's gauge/Minkowski functional or an infimum-based definition with |0|_K = 0, then prove the attained-minimum characterization only for x nonzero.

items.label: Sec. 1, Eq. (1.1)
items.name: Successive minima of a convex body with respect to the integer lattice

human.statement: Sec. 1, Eq. (1.1) and the sentence following it

items.statement_informal: For an origin-symmetric body, the i-th successive minimum is the smallest dilation factor for which the dilated body contains i linearly independent integer points. For a general body the definition is applied to its central symmetral.
items.statement_formal: For K = -K in K^n and 1 <= i <= n, lambda_i(K) = min { lambda > 0 : dim(lambda K intersect Z^n) >= i }. For general K in K^n, lambda_i(K) := lambda_i(cs(K)) where cs(K) = (1/2)(K - K).
items.proof_as_in_paper: A definition. The paper does not argue that the minimum is attained; the min is written rather than an inf.
items.proof_completeness: definition
known_issues_in_paper: Eq. (1.1) writes min rather than inf; attainment holds because the set of admissible dilation factors is closed under the compactness of K, but the paper does not say so.

lean.route_note: The source's symmetric-body formula is restated in its dilation notation and instantiated for the coordinate-box equality family; the formal definition uses the corresponding infimum until its attainment is proved.

items.label: Sec. 2, third paragraph
items.name: The successive minima expressed through the gauge of the central symmetral

human.statement: Sec. 2, paragraph beginning 'If K satisfies -K = K, its gauge function'

background_notation.|x|_K: gauge of an origin-symmetric body K, min { r > 0 : x in rK }
background_notation.|x|_cs(K): gauge of the central symmetral, the notation the paper writes as |x|_{cs(K)}

items.statement_informal: The paper claims that the successive minima can be recovered recursively from gauge values outside the span generated at the preceding minimum.
items.statement_formal: lambda_1(K) = min { |z|_cs(K) : z in Z^n, z nonzero }, and for i >= 2, lambda_i(K) = min { |z|_cs(K) : z in Z^n outside span(lambda_{i-1}(K) cs(K) intersect Z^n) }.
items.proof_as_in_paper: Stated as an alternative to Eq. (1.1); the equivalence is not argued.
items.proof_technique: Equivalence of a dilation description and a gauge description of the same infimum.
items.proof_completeness: literal-reading conflict: the recurrence is false when consecutive minima coincide; Eq. (1.1) remains the valid definition

Thus the recursive formula is false as written whenever the preceding minimum already spans too large a subspace; no strict-minima hypothesis is part of the paper.
items.formalization_notes: Use Eq. (1.1) as the definition. Prove the gauge characterization through a greedy flag or through the threshold subspaces span({z in Z^n : |z|_cs(K) <= r}), so repeated minima are handled without adding lambda_{i-1} < lambda_i.

items.label: Sec. 1 and Sec. 2, notation
items.name: Lattices and the lattice point enumerator

human.statement: Sec. 1, sentence introducing G(K); Sec. 2, paragraph 'A lattice ... is the integral span'

background_notation.G_Lambda(A): number of points of the lattice Lambda in the set A

items.statement_informal: A lattice is the integral span of linearly independent vectors; the lattice point enumerator counts the lattice points of a set, and the unsubscripted enumerator refers to the integer lattice.
items.statement_formal: Lambda = { sum_{i=1}^k m_i x_i : m_i in Z } for linearly independent x_1, ..., x_k in R^n; G_Lambda(A) = card(A intersect Lambda); G(A) = G_{Z^n}(A).
items.proof_as_in_paper: A definition.
items.proof_completeness: definition

lean.route_note: The enumerator equals the cardinality of the finite lattice intersection for compact sets and discrete lattices. Integral spans are identified with integer linear combinations. Positive body dilation is identified exactly with reciprocal lattice refinement, both at set and cardinality level.

items.label: Sec. 2, sentence after the lattice definition
items.name: The projection of a lattice along a sublattice span is again a lattice

human.statement: Sec. 2, sentence 'We will use that for any X subseteq Lambda, the set Lambda|span(X)^perp is also a lattice'

background_notation.A|L: image of the orthogonal projection of A onto the linear subspace L

hypotheses: Lambda is a lattice in R^n.
X is a subset of Lambda.
items.statement_informal: Projecting a lattice orthogonally along the span of any subset of its own points leaves a lattice.
items.statement_formal: For a lattice Lambda in R^n and X subseteq Lambda, the image Lambda|span(X)^perp is a lattice.
items.proof_as_in_paper: Asserted as a fact that will be used; no proof is given.
items.proof_completeness: asserted, not derived
known_issues_in_paper: The statement is true because span(X) is spanned by lattice vectors, which makes the projected group discrete. Projecting along the span of an arbitrary subspace does not give a lattice, so the hypothesis X subseteq Lambda carries the whole content and is easy to lose.

lean.route_note: The projection image is now a Z-submodule of the orthogonal-complement subtype. Its induced topology is discrete and its real span is the full subtype; these are instantiated locally to obtain a positive covolume. The ambient/projected covolume comparison belongs to the separate projection-determinant item.

items.label: Sec. 3, opening paragraph
items.name: Anti-blocking convex body

human.statement: Sec. 3, first paragraph

background_notation.e_i^perp: the coordinate hyperplane orthogonal to e_i

hypotheses: K is a convex body contained in the non-negative orthant.
items.statement_informal: A convex body in the non-negative orthant is anti-blocking when it is downward closed: every point dominated coordinatewise by a point of the body is again in the body. For a convex body this is the same as saying that intersecting with a coordinate hyperplane and projecting onto it give the same set.
items.statement_formal: K subseteq R^n_{>=0} is anti-blocking iff for every x in K the set { x' in R^n_{>=0} : x'_i <= x_i for all i in [n] } is contained in K; equivalently, given convexity, K intersect e_i^perp = K|e_i^perp for all i in [n].
items.proof_as_in_paper: A definition together with an equivalence stated as immediate from convexity; the equivalence is not proved.
items.proof_technique: Coordinatewise domination versus fibrewise projection.
items.proof_completeness: asserted, not derived

items.name: Blaschke shaking with respect to an oriented hyperplane

human.statement: Sec. 3, unnumbered display following Theorem 3.1, with Fig. 1

background_notation.sh_u(K): the Blaschke shaking of K with respect to u
background_notation.f_{u,K}(x): the length of the preimage of x under the orthogonal projection of K onto u^perp

hypotheses: u is a non-zero vector of R^n.
items.statement_informal: The shaking of a body pushes each of its fibres in the direction u down onto the hyperplane orthogonal to u, keeping the fibre's length. The result is the union of segments starting on the projection of the body.

items.proof_as_in_paper: A definition, with a figure showing two consecutive shakings.
items.proof_completeness: definition

items.label: Sec. 1, Eq. (1.2)
items.name: Minkowski's second theorem on successive minima
items.kind_note: Classical result of other authors, quoted by the paper and used in the proofs of Corollary 1.2, Proposition 1.5 and Theorem 1.4.
items.statement_informal: The volume of a convex body is bounded above and below by the product of the reciprocals of its successive minima, up to the factorial factor on the lower side.
items.statement_formal: (1/n!) prod_{i=1}^n (2/lambda_i(K)) <= vol(K) <= prod_{i=1}^n (2/lambda_i(K)).
items.proof_as_in_paper: Not proved here. The paper attributes the origin-symmetric case to Minkowski, derives the general upper bound from vol(K) <= vol(cs(K)), itself a special case of the Brunn-Minkowski inequality, and points to an inclusion argument through the convex hull of the n segments realizing the minima for the general lower bound. It lists alternative proofs by Davenport, Weyl, Estermann, Bambah-Woods-Zassenhaus and Henk.
items.proof_technique: Quoted classical theorem. The general upper bound is reduced to the symmetric theorem through the central symmetral; the general lower bound uses the cross-polytope contained in the convex hull of segments realizing the minima.
items.proof_completeness: relies on external Minkowski, Geometry of Numbers, Ch. 2, Theorems 9.1 and 9.2, plus Brunn-Minkowski for the non-symmetric upper bound and Henk-Henze-Hernandez Cifre, Remark 1.1, for the non-symmetric lower bound
external_dependencies: Minkowski's second theorem for origin-symmetric bodies, as in Gruber and Lekkerkerker, Geometry of Numbers, Ch. 2, Theorems 9.1 and 9.2.
The Brunn-Minkowski inequality, in the form vol(K) <= vol(cs(K)).
Henk, Henze and Hernandez Cifre, Remark 1.1, for the non-symmetric lower bound.

lean.route_note: Both halves of Eq. (1.2) are assembled in the paper's reciprocal-minima normalization. The lower bound uses the segments realizing the minima. The upper bound specializes the pinned Minkowski theorem to the standard lattice and converts its product normalization using covolume one. The pinned upper proof uses squeezing and Blichfeldt rather than a reduction through the central symmetral. Dimension zero is included.

items.proof_completeness: asserted, not derived

items.label: Sec. 1, unnumbered display before Conjecture 1
items.name: The Betke-Henk-Wills two-sided bound on the lattice point enumerator
items.kind_note: Result of other authors, quoted as the starting point of the whole line of work. The version of record prints this display without a number.

human.statement: Sec. 1, unnumbered display immediately before Conjecture 1

hypotheses: K is in K^n with K = -K.
For the lower bound only, lambda_n(K) <= 2.
items.statement_informal: For an origin-symmetric body the number of lattice points is bounded on both sides by products in the successive minima.
items.statement_formal: (1/n!) prod_{i=1}^n (1/lambda_i(K) - 1) <= G(K) <= prod_{i=1}^n (2 i / lambda_i(K) + 1), the lower bound under lambda_n(K) <= 2.
items.proof_as_in_paper: Not proved here; attributed to Betke, Henk and Wills, Proposition 2.1 and Corollary 2.1. Their Proposition 2.1 gives the displayed upper bound, but their Corollary 2.1 has the stronger lower factors 2/lambda_i-1, not the target paper's printed 1/lambda_i-1. The target then says its printed lower bound is best possible.
items.proof_completeness: the upper bound relies on external Betke, Henk and Wills, Proposition 2.1; the printed lower bound is true but is not the cited Corollary 2.1 and its best-possible claim is false
external_dependencies: Betke, Henk and Wills, Discrete Comput. Geom. 9 (1993), Proposition 2.1 and Corollary 2.1.
known_issues_in_paper: The cited Betke-Henk-Wills Corollary 2.1 has factors 2/lambda_i-1, whereas the target display prints 1/lambda_i-1. These normalizations agree neither for the target's origin-symmetric K nor under its definition of central symmetral.

Consequently the sentence 'the lower bound is best-possible' is false for the displayed lower bound: the cited source itself gives a strictly stronger universal lower estimate. Under lambda_n <= 2 the printed lower bound can instead be proved directly from 0 in K intersect Z^n, since a negative product is trivial and a positive product is at most 1.
items.formalization_notes: Formalize the literal target display as printed and separately prove the exact stronger primary-source Corollary 2.1 in the dependency layer. Do not silently replace the target's factor 1 by 2, and do not formalize the false best-possible sentence as a theorem.

lean.route_note: Quoted contextual result: formal statement only under the recorded scope, not a theorem claim.

items.label: Conjecture 1
items.name: Betke-Henk-Wills conjecture on the lattice point enumerator
items.kind_note: The paper states this as an open conjecture and does not prove it. Its display is unnumbered in the version of record.

human.statement: Conjecture 1

background_notation.floor(x): the largest integer not exceeding x

items.statement_informal: The number of lattice points of a convex body is conjectured to be at most the product of the floors of 2/lambda_i + 1.
items.statement_formal: G(K) <= prod_{i=1}^n floor(2/lambda_i(K) + 1).
items.proof_as_in_paper: No proof; the paper records that the conjecture is confirmed in dimension 2 by Betke, Henk and Wills and in dimension 3 by Malikiosis. The primary sources prove those dimensional cases only for origin-symmetric bodies, so the two exact established subcases are cataloged separately. Its integer-box equality witness is also cataloged separately.
items.proof_completeness: asserted as an open conjecture; not derived
external_dependencies: Betke, Henk and Wills, Conjecture 2.1, for the statement; their Theorem 2.2 for the planar case; Malikiosis, Section 3.2, for dimension 3.
known_issues_in_paper: As stated here, Conjecture 1 allows arbitrary convex bodies because lambda_i(K) is defined through the central symmetral. Betke-Henk-Wills Theorem 2.2 and Malikiosis Section 3.2 prove only the origin-symmetric cases in dimensions 2 and 3. Thus the sentence that 'the conjecture' as printed has been confirmed in those dimensions overstates the cited results.

lean.route_note: State as a proposition expressing an open conjecture; do not assert it as an axiom or theorem.

items.label: Sec. 1, Eq. (1.3)
items.name: Malikiosis's bound on the lattice point enumerator
items.kind_note: Result of another author, quoted as the best known general bound at the time of writing.
items.statement_informal: The lattice point count is at most an exponential factor times the conjectured product.
items.statement_formal: G(K) <= (4/e) (sqrt 3)^{n-1} prod_{i=1}^n (2/lambda_i(K) + 1).
items.proof_as_in_paper: Not proved here; quoted from Malikiosis, Theorem 3.2.1 in the journal numbering. The arXiv v1 source numbers it Theorem 3.1.2 and proves the stronger integer-part form G(K,Lambda) <= (4/e)(sqrt 3)^{n-1} prod_i floor(2/lambda_i(K,Lambda)+1); dropping the floors gives exactly the displayed target-paper inequality. The paper notes this remains the best known upper bound in general dimension and compares it with Corollary 1.2: the bound here is of order n^n while Malikiosis's is of order sqrt(3)^n when all lambda_i(K) equal a fixed 1/c.
items.proof_completeness: relies on external Malikiosis, Adv. Geom. 12 (2012), Theorem 3.2.1 (arXiv v1 Theorem 3.1.2), followed by floor(x) <= x
external_dependencies: Malikiosis, A discrete analogue for Minkowski's second theorem on successive minima, journal Theorem 3.2.1 / arXiv:1001.3729v1 Theorem 3.1.2.
items.formalization_notes: Formalize the stronger primary-source theorem with q_i = floor(2/lambda_i + 1), then derive the target paper's floor-free Eq. (1.3) by factorwise monotonicity. Do not present the two displays as verbatim identical.

lean.route_note: Quoted contextual bound: formal statement only under the recorded scope; distinct from the established dimension-three subcase.

items.label: Sec. 1, Eq. (1.4) and the paragraph following it
items.name: Any bound of the form prod (2/lambda_i + c_i) implies Minkowski's upper bound

human.statement: Sec. 1, Eq. (1.4) and the paragraph following it

background_notation.c_i: constants independent of K, but allowed to depend on n

hypotheses: The bound G(K) <= prod_{i=1}^n (2/lambda_i(K) + c_i) holds for all K in K^n with constants c_i independent of K.
items.statement_informal: A bound on the lattice point count of that shape, with constants that do not depend on the body, forces Minkowski's upper bound on the volume, because the volume is approximated by lattice point counts with respect to progressively finer lattices.
items.statement_formal: If G(K) <= prod_{i=1}^n (2/lambda_i(K) + c_i) for all K in K^n, then vol(K) <= prod_{i=1}^n (2/lambda_i(K)) for all K in K^n.
items.proof_as_in_paper: The paper gives the argument in one sentence and attributes it to Betke, Henk and Wills, Proposition 2.2: one approximates the volume of K asymptotically by the lattice point enumerator with respect to progressively finer lattices, using the properties of the Riemann integral, applies the assumed bound to each, and the resulting limit is precisely Minkowski's bound.
items.proof_technique: Refining the lattice, Jordan measurability, and the scaling law of the minima under a refined lattice.
items.proof_completeness: asserted, not derived; the limiting argument is described but not written out
external_dependencies: Betke, Henk and Wills, Proposition 2.2.
known_issues_in_paper: The step that the successive minima scale under lattice refinement, lambda_i(K, rZ^n) = r lambda_i(K, Z^n), is used silently.

lean.route_note: The terminal product_bound_implies_minkowski assumes the paper's universal standard-lattice count bound with arbitrary body-independent constants. The earlier arbitrary-lattice implication is retained as a supplemental theorem with its explicit refined-lattice premise, not as the terminal paper statement.

human.statement: Conjecture 2

items.statement_informal: The ratio between the lattice point count and the volume is conjectured to be controlled on both sides by products in the successive minima, weighted by the index.
items.statement_formal: (1.5) G(K) <= vol(K) prod_{i=1}^n (1 + i lambda_i / 2); (1.6) if lambda_n <= 2/n then G(int K) >= vol(K) prod_{i=1}^n (1 - i lambda_i / 2); (1.7) if K = -K and lambda_n <= 2 then G(int K) >= vol(K) prod_{i=1}^n (1 - lambda_i / 2).
items.proof_as_in_paper: No proof. The paper notes that Eq. (1.7) is stated in Betke, Henk and Wills for arbitrary n-dimensional lattices and that restricting to Z^n loses no generality, and that Eqs. (1.5) and (1.6) came from Martin Henk personally.
items.proof_completeness: asserted as an open conjecture; not derived

items.label: Theorem 1.1, Eq. (1.8)
items.name: Upper bound on the lattice point enumerator by the volume and the successive minima

human.statement: Theorem 1.1, Eq. (1.8)
human.proof: Sec. 4, Proof of Theorem 1.1, first half

background_notation.L_I: the coordinate subspace spanned by the e_i with i in I

items.statement_informal: The number of lattice points of a convex body is at most its volume times the product of 1 + n lambda_i / 2.
items.statement_formal: G(K) <= vol(K) prod_{i=1}^n (1 + n lambda_i(K) / 2).
items.proof_as_in_paper: By Theorem 3.1 one may assume K anti-blocking, and after renumbering coordinates that |e_i|_cs(K) = lambda_i by Lemma 3.3. For I subseteq [n] put L_I = span{ e_i : i in I }. The Rogers-Shephard inequality (4.1) gives vol_k(K intersect L_I) vol_{n-k}(K|L_I^perp) <= binom(n,k) vol(K) for I of size k. Lemma 3.3 gives (2/lambda_i) e_i in K, so vol_k(K intersect L_I) >= vol_k(conv{ (2/lambda_i) e_i : i in I }), whence vol_{n-k}(K|L_I^perp) <= binom(n,k) vol(K) / vol_k(conv{...}) = k! binom(n,k) vol(K) prod_{i in I} (lambda_i / 2) <= vol(K) prod_{i in I} (n lambda_i / 2). Combining with Davenport's inequality (1.10), G(K) <= vol(K) sum_{I subseteq [n]} prod_{i in I} (n lambda_i / 2) = vol(K) prod_{i=1}^n (1 + n lambda_i / 2).
items.proof_technique: Reduction to an anti-blocking body, Rogers-Shephard section-projection inequality, the simplex spanned by (2/lambda_i) e_i, then Davenport's inequality and the expansion of a product into subset sums.
items.proof_completeness: self-contained given theorem_3_1_anti_blocking_reduction and lemma_3_3_minima_at_standard_basis, relying on external rogers_shephard_section_projection and davenport_inequality
external_dependencies: Rogers and Shephard, Theorem 1, the section-projection inequality, cataloged as rogers_shephard_section_projection.
Davenport's inequality, cataloged as davenport_inequality; for anti-blocking bodies the paper also re-derives it internally, cataloged as davenport_for_anti_blocking_bodies.
known_issues_in_paper: The chain uses k! binom(n,k) <= n^k, which holds for 0 <= k <= n, without stating it.

The volume of conv{ (2/lambda_i) e_i : i in I } is (1/k!) prod_{i in I} (2/lambda_i), the volume of a k-dimensional simplex with those vertices and the origin; the origin is a vertex because K is anti-blocking, and the paper does not say so explicitly.

The reduction to an anti-blocking body changes the successive minima, so the final product must be monotone in each lambda_i; this is true for the upper bound because lambda_i(A) <= lambda_i(K), and the step is left implicit.

items.label: Theorem 1.1, Eq. (1.9)
items.name: Lower bound on the interior lattice point enumerator by the volume and the successive minima

human.statement: Theorem 1.1, Eq. (1.9)
human.proof: Sec. 4, Proof of Theorem 1.1, second half

items.statement_informal: Under a smallness hypothesis on the largest successive minimum, the number of interior lattice points is at least the volume times the product of 1 - n lambda_i / 2.
items.statement_formal: If lambda_n(K) <= 2/n then G(int K) >= vol(K) prod_{i=1}^n (1 - n lambda_i(K) / 2).
items.proof_as_in_paper: Uses the covering-radius lower bound (1.16) together with the relation (4.2), mu(K) <= sum_{i=1}^n lambda_i / 2. Since lambda_n <= 2/n, (4.2) gives mu(K) <= 1, so Proposition 1.6 applies and G(int K) >= vol(K)(1 - mu(K))^n >= vol(K)(1 - sum_i lambda_i / 2)^n = vol(K) ((1/n) sum_i (1 - n lambda_i / 2))^n >= vol(K) prod_{i=1}^n (1 - n lambda_i / 2), the last step by the inequality of arithmetic and geometric means.
items.proof_technique: Covering-radius bound, the covering-radius versus successive-minima inequality, then arithmetic-geometric mean.
items.proof_completeness: self-contained given proposition_1_6_lower_bound, relying on external covering_radius_successive_minima_bound
external_dependencies: Kannan and Lovasz, Covering minima and lattice point free convex bodies, Lemma 2.4, cataloged as covering_radius_successive_minima_bound.
known_issues_in_paper: The arithmetic-geometric mean step needs each factor 1 - n lambda_i / 2 to be non-negative, which follows from lambda_n <= 2/n and the monotonicity of the minima; the paper does not state it.
The proof of Eq. (1.9) does not go through the anti-blocking reduction, although the sentence introducing Sec. 3 says the reduction suffices for Eqs. (1.5) and (1.6).

lean.route_note: Includes the paper's smallness hypothesis on the last successive minimum. Compactness and IsPaperConvexBody together express the paper's body class.

human.statement: Corollary 1.2, with the comparison paragraph that follows

items.label: Sec. 1, Eq. (1.10)
items.name: Davenport's inequality bounding the enumerator by projection volumes
items.kind_note: Result of another author, used in the proof of Theorem 1.1.

human.statement: Sec. 1, Eq. (1.10), with the sentence defining L_I

background_notation.K|L_I^perp: the orthogonal projection of K onto the orthogonal complement of L_I

items.statement_informal: Davenport's intended inequality bounds the number of lattice points by the sum of the volumes of all coordinate projections, including the body itself for the empty coordinate subset.
items.statement_formal: G(K) <= sum_{k=0}^n sum_{I in binom([n],k)} vol_{n-k}(K|L_I^perp), where L_I = span{ e_i : i in I } and the k = 0 term is vol_n(K).
items.proof_as_in_paper: Not proved here; quoted from Davenport, On a principle of Lipschitz. Davenport's theorem gives |G(K)-vol_n(K)| <= sum_{m=0}^{n-1} V_m for a convex body (his fibre parameter h is 1), where V_m is the sum of all m-dimensional coordinate-projection volumes and V_0 = 1. Keeping the positive side and adding vol_n(K) gives exactly the intended all-subsets formula. For anti-blocking bodies, which is the case actually used, the target paper also gives a direct derivation, cataloged as davenport_for_anti_blocking_bodies.
items.proof_completeness: relies on external Davenport, J. London Math. Soc. 26 (1951), 179-183
external_dependencies: Davenport, On a principle of Lipschitz, J. London Math. Soc. 26 (1951).
known_issues_in_paper: Eq. (1.10) is printed with k = 1, omitting the necessary k = 0 term vol_n(K). The literal formula is false already for n = 1 and K = [0,1], where G(K) = 2 but the printed right-hand side is vol_0({0}) = 1. The cited inequality and the paper's later anti-blocking decomposition both require k = 0.
items.formalization_notes: Formalize the intended k = 0 through n theorem and retain the printed k = 1 formula only as a documented source discrepancy; do not add a hypothesis to rescue the literal formula. The index bridge is m = n-k: Davenport's V_m becomes the inner sum over |I| = k.

lean.route_note: The general all-coordinate-subsets upper bound is proved for every compact convex set. The proof uses successive coordinate shakings: lattice count increases, each intrinsic projection volume decreases, and the final anti-blocking body satisfies the paper's prism bound. This is an alternative derivation of the quoted upper bound; it does not mechanize Davenport's two-sided discrepancy induction. Source-route disposition remains subject to the faithfulness audit.

items.label: Sec. 1, Eq. (1.11)
items.name: Schymura's generalization of Davenport's inequality to an arbitrary independent set
items.kind_note: Result of another author; Theorem 1.3 is its reverse.

hypotheses: b_1, ..., b_n is a linearly independent set in Z^n.

items.statement_formal: G(K) <= sum_{k=0}^n sum_{I in binom([n],k)} vol_{n-k}(K|L_I^perp) vol_k(P_I), where L_I = span{ b_i : i in I }, P_I = sum_{i in I} [0, b_i], and the k = 0 term is vol_n(K).
items.proof_as_in_paper: Not proved here; quoted as Schymura's Lemma 1.1. The cited paper was published under the name Matthias Henze and its Lemma 1.1 explicitly sums from i = 0 to n.
items.proof_completeness: relies on external Henze (cited as Schymura), Lemma 1.1
external_dependencies: Matthias Henze, A Blichfeldt-type inequality for centrally symmetric convex bodies, Lemma 1.1 (arXiv:1203.4075v1; cited in this paper as Schymura).

items.label: Theorem 1.3, Eq. (1.12)
items.name: A reverse form of Schymura's inequality: the volume is bounded by projected enumerators

human.statement: Theorem 1.3, Eq. (1.12)
human.proof: Sec. 4, Proof of Theorem 1.3

background_notation.G_{Z^n|L_I^perp}: the lattice point enumerator with respect to the projected lattice Z^n|L_I^perp

hypotheses: b_1, ..., b_n is a linearly independent set in Z^n.
items.statement_informal: The volume of a convex body is at most the sum, over all coordinate subsets including the empty one, of the numbers of projected lattice points in the corresponding projections of its interior.
items.statement_formal: vol(K) <= sum_{I subseteq [n]} G_{Z^n|L_I^perp}(int K | L_I^perp), where L_I = span{ b_i : i in I }.
items.proof_as_in_paper: The proof proves Claim 3, a bound on the enumerator of a translate, and then applies van der Corput's Theorem 2.1. Claim 3 with Lambda = Z^n, B = { b_1, ..., b_n } and an arbitrary t gives G(int K + t) <= sum_{I subseteq [n]} G_{Z^n|L_I^perp}(int K | L_I^perp), Eq. (4.6) in the source text, valid for every t; van der Corput's theorem supplies a t with vol(int K) <= G(int K + t), and vol(int K) = vol(K).
items.proof_technique: Induction on the support of the translation vector (Claim 3), then van der Corput's averaging theorem to choose the translate.
items.proof_completeness: self-contained given claim_3_translation_projection_bound, relying on external van_der_corput_theorem
external_dependencies: van der Corput's theorem, cataloged as van_der_corput_theorem.
known_issues_in_paper: Eq. (1.12) is stated for K in K^n, hence compact, while the interior enters on the right; the step vol(K) = vol(int K) is used silently.
Eq. (1.12) correctly runs over every I subseteq [n], including the empty set. The contrast with the printed k = 1 in Eq. (1.11) is further evidence that Eq. (1.11) omitted its k = 0 term.

lean.route_note: First proved using quotient-class counts, then identified exactly with orthogonal-projection counts. The theorem does not require the chosen independent vectors to be integral.

items.label: Sec. 4, final display of the Proof of Theorem 1.3
items.name: The reverse inequality is attained by axis-parallel integer boxes

human.statement: Theorem 1.3, sentence 'The inequality is tight'
human.proof: Sec. 4, final display of the Proof of Theorem 1.3

hypotheses: K = [0, k_1] x ... x [0, k_n] with positive integers k_i.
items.statement_informal: For an axis-parallel box with positive integer side lengths and the standard basis, the reverse inequality holds with equality.
items.statement_formal: For K = [0,k_1] x ... x [0,k_n] with k_i in Z_{>0}, vol(K) = prod_i k_i = prod_i ((k_i - 1) + 1) = sum_{I subseteq [n]} prod_{i in I} (k_i - 1) = sum_{I subseteq [n]} G_{Z^n|L_I^perp}(int K | L_I^perp).
items.proof_as_in_paper: The displayed computation expands the product of (k_i - 1) + 1 into a subset sum and then identifies the total with the sum of the interior lattice-point counts of the corresponding projections.
items.proof_technique: Expansion of a product into subset sums.
items.proof_completeness: self-contained
known_issues_in_paper: Projection onto L_I^perp retains the coordinates j not in I, so G_{Z^n|L_I^perp}(int K | L_I^perp) = prod_{j notin I}(k_j - 1), not prod_{i in I}(k_i - 1) term by term as the displayed chain suggests. The two total sums agree by the complement bijection I maps to [n] without I. The projected lattice is the standard coordinate lattice Z^{n-|I|}.
items.formalization_notes: Prove the projected count with the complement indices, then reindex the finite sum by set complement before applying the product expansion.

items.label: Sec. 1, sentence after Theorem 1.3
items.name: The determinant of the projected lattice absorbs Schymura's zonotope factor

human.statement: Sec. 1, sentence 'The factor vol_k(P_I) in (1.11) is hidden in the correspondingly higher density'

hypotheses: b_1, ..., b_n is a linearly independent set in Z^n.
items.statement_informal: The projected lattice is at least as dense as the reciprocal of the volume of the zonotope generated by the chosen vectors.
items.statement_formal: det(Z^n|L_I^perp) >= vol_k(P_I)^{-1}, where k = card(I).
items.proof_as_in_paper: Asserted in one sentence; no proof.
items.proof_completeness: asserted, not derived
items.formalization_notes: The direction is correct. If Lambda_I = Z^n intersect L_I is the primitive lattice in L_I, then det(Z^n|L_I^perp) = 1/det(Lambda_I). The lattice generated by the b_i, i in I, is a sublattice of Lambda_I, so vol_k(P_I) is an integer index times det(Lambda_I), giving det(Z^n|L_I^perp) >= 1/vol_k(P_I).

lean.route_note: The selected independent integer vectors are a real basis of their Euclidean subspace; their zonotope has intrinsic parallelepiped volume. Integral splitting supplies arbitrary lifts of a projected basis. An adapted-basis block determinant gives ambient covolume = full-section covolume times projected covolume. The lattice-index theorem compares the selected-vector lattice with the full intersection, without a primitivity assumption. The standard integer lattice has covolume one, and the intrinsic orthogonal image is identified with the paper's projected lattice.

items.label: Sec. 1, the two unnumbered Ehrhart displays
items.name: Integer multiples of the standard simplex attain both bounds of Conjecture 2

human.statement: Sec. 1, paragraph beginning 'In fact, all inequalities in Conjecture 2 have equality cases', with its two unnumbered displays

background_notation.T_n: the standard simplex conv{0, e_1, ..., e_n}

items.statement_informal: For integer dilates of the standard simplex both conjectured bounds hold with equality, because the right-hand sides coincide with the Ehrhart polynomial of the simplex and with its interior counterpart.
items.statement_formal: For every i in [n], lambda_i(T_n) = 2 and lambda_i(m T_n) = 2/m. Moreover G(m T_n) = (1/n!) prod_{i=1}^n (m + i) = vol(m T_n) prod_{i=1}^n (1 + i lambda_i(m T_n)/2), while G(int(m T_n)) = (1/n!) prod_{i=1}^n (m - i) = vol(m T_n) prod_{i=1}^n (1 - i lambda_i(m T_n)/2).
items.proof_as_in_paper: The two displayed computations use lambda_i(T_n) = 2, scaling lambda_i(mT_n) = 2/m, vol(mT_n) = m^n/n!, and the closed and interior Ehrhart formulas for the standard simplex from Beck and Robins, Theorem 2.2 (a) and (b). The author-hosted final draft was checked directly: Theorem 2.2(a) states L_Delta(t) = binom(d+t,d), while part (b) identifies the interior count by reciprocity.
items.proof_technique: Ehrhart polynomial of the standard simplex, and the scaling of the successive minima.
items.proof_completeness: self-contained given the Ehrhart polynomial of the standard simplex
external_dependencies: Beck and Robins, Computing the continuum discretely, Theorem 2.2 (a) and (b).

For 1 <= m <= n, the interior formula is still correct: both sides vanish because the product contains the factor m - m. This small-scale case is not discussed separately.
items.formalization_notes: Prove the two lattice-point counts directly by stars and bars and prove lambda_i(T_n) = 2 from coordinate bounds on T_n - T_n. This yields the exact equality case without importing general Ehrhart theory.

items.label: Theorem 1.4, Eq. (1.13)
items.name: The planar case of the conjectured upper bound

human.statement: Theorem 1.4, Eq. (1.13)
human.proof: Sec. 5, Proof of Theorem 1.4, first half

background_notation.l_t: the horizontal line at height t

items.statement_informal: In the plane the conjectured upper bound holds as stated.
items.statement_formal: G(K) <= vol(K) (1 + lambda_1(K)/2)(1 + lambda_2(K)).
items.proof_as_in_paper: By Theorem 3.1 and Lemma 5.1 one may assume K anti-blocking with |e_i|_cs(K) = lambda_i and K contained in the half plane x_1 + x_2 <= 2/lambda_1. Let f(t) = vol_1(K intersect l_t) on [0, 2/lambda_2]; f is concave since K is convex, decreasing since K is anti-blocking, and satisfies Eq. (5.3), f(t) <= f(0) - t = 2/lambda_1 - t. Counting by horizontal lattice lines, G(K) = sum_{i=0}^{floor(2/lambda_2)} G(K intersect l_i) <= sum (f(i) + 1), which regroups as (1/2)(f(0) + f(floor(2/lambda_2))) + sum_{i=1}^{floor(2/lambda_2)} (1/2)(f(i-1) + f(i)) + floor(2/lambda_2) + 1. Applying Eq. (5.3) to f(floor(2/lambda_2)) and the lower bound of Lemma 5.2 to each trapezoid gives G(K) <= 2/lambda_1 - (1/2) floor(2/lambda_2) + integral_0^{floor(2/lambda_2)} f + floor(2/lambda_2) + 1 <= vol(K) + 2/lambda_1 + 1/lambda_2 + 1 <= vol(K)(1 + lambda_2 + lambda_1/2 + lambda_1 lambda_2 / 2) = vol(K)(1 + lambda_1/2)(1 + lambda_2), where the third line uses the lower bound of Minkowski's second theorem applied to each of the summands 2/lambda_1, 1/lambda_2 and 1.
items.proof_technique: Reduction to an anti-blocking body under a diagonal, slicing by horizontal lattice lines, trapezoid estimate for a concave section function, then Minkowski's lower bound to convert additive error terms into multiplicative ones.
items.proof_completeness: self-contained given theorem_3_1_anti_blocking_reduction, lemma_5_1_properties_of_the_planar_reduction, lemma_5_2_concave_integral_bounds, diagonal_section_bound and minkowski_second_theorem
external_dependencies: The lower bound of Minkowski's second theorem, cataloged as minkowski_second_theorem.
known_issues_in_paper: The first display of the proof writes the summand as G(K intersect l_t) with t while the summation index is i; the intended reading is l_i.

The next displayed rearrangement has an unmatched opening parenthesis after the factor 1/2. The following line shows the intended grouping: only f(0) + f(floor(2/lambda_2)) is halved, while the trapezoid sum and floor(2/lambda_2) + 1 remain outside.

The count over horizontal lattice lines runs from 0 to floor(2/lambda_2), which presumes that the body meets no horizontal lattice line above that height; this uses h(K, e_2) = 2/lambda_2, stated one line earlier for the anti-blocking body.
The step G(K intersect l_i) <= f(i) + 1 is the one-dimensional count on a segment of length f(i) and is used without comment.

human.statement: Theorem 1.4, Eq. (1.14)

items.statement_informal: In the plane the number of interior lattice points is at least the volume times 1 - lambda_1/2 - lambda_2.
items.statement_formal: G(int K) >= vol(K) (1 - lambda_1(K)/2 - lambda_2(K)).
items.proof_as_in_paper: Same reduction and same section function f, assumed differentiable after an approximation from below by a smooth concave function. The highest horizontal integer line meeting int K is at height ceil(2/lambda_2 - 1), so G(int K) = sum_{i=1}^{ceil(2/lambda_2 -1)} G(int K intersect l_i) >= sum (f(i) - 1). The upper bound of Lemma 5.2 gives f(i) >= integral_i^{i+1} f - (1/2) f'(i) for i < ceil(2/lambda_2 - 1) and a corresponding estimate on the last, shorter interval. Summing gives Eq. (5.4), whose integral part is vol(K) - integral_0^1 f. Eq. (5.5) bounds integral_0^1 f <= 2/lambda_1 - 1/2 using Eq. (5.3). The bracket of derivative terms is bounded below by integral_0^{2/lambda_2 - 1} (-f') = f(0) - f(2/lambda_2 - 1) >= 2/lambda_2 - 1, using that -f' is increasing and non-negative and Eq. (5.3) again. Substituting yields G(int K) >= vol(K) - 2/lambda_1 + 1/2 + (1/2)(2/lambda_2 - 1) - ceil(2/lambda_2 - 1) >= vol(K) - 2/lambda_1 - 1/lambda_2 = vol(K)(1 - (1/vol(K))(2/lambda_1 + 1/lambda_2)) >= vol(K)(1 - lambda_1/2 - lambda_2), the last step using vol(K) >= 2/(lambda_1 lambda_2).
items.proof_technique: Slicing by horizontal lattice lines, tangent estimate for a concave section function, monotonicity of the derivative, and Minkowski's lower bound in the plane.
items.proof_completeness: gap: the smooth concave approximation from below and the limiting transfer to the original section function are described but not proved

known_issues_in_paper: Differentiability of f is assumed and justified by a two-step approximation, first by a linear spline from below and then by rounding corners; the approximating body K' is said to satisfy g(0) = f(0) and to lie under the diagonal, and the passage to the limit is not written out.
In Eq. (5.4) the upper limit of the last integral is printed as lambda_2/2 where the argument requires 2/lambda_2; the surrounding lines use 2/lambda_2 consistently.
The estimate f(i) >= integral_i^{i+1} f - (1/2) f'(i) applies Lemma 5.2 on the interval [i, i+1] and uses that -f'(i) >= 0; the sign convention is easy to lose.

items.label: Proposition 1.6, Eq. (1.15)
items.name: Covering-radius upper bound on the lattice point enumerator

human.statement: Proposition 1.6, Eq. (1.15)
human.proof: Sec. 4, Proof of Proposition 1.6, first half

items.statement_informal: The number of lattice points of a convex body is at most its volume times (1 + covering radius) to the power n.
items.statement_formal: G(K) <= vol(K) (1 + mu(K))^n.
items.proof_as_in_paper: It suffices to exhibit a measurable S contained in mu K with S + Z^n = R^n and int S disjoint from all its non-zero integer translates, because then G(K) = vol((K intersect Z^n) + S) <= vol(K + mu K) = (1 + mu)^n vol(K). To build S, let P = [0,1]^n and take finitely many translates mu K + x_i, x_i in Z^n, covering P. Set P_1 = P intersect (mu K + x_1) and inductively P_i = (P minus the union of the earlier P_j) intersect (mu K + x_i); let S_i = P_i - x_i, contained in mu K, and S the union of the S_i. The P_i are interiorly disjoint and cover P, so the S_i are interiorly disjoint and vol(S) = vol(P) = 1; and if int S met int S + x for an integer x, two of the P_i would overlap after an integer translation, forcing x = 0.
items.proof_technique: Construction of a measurable fundamental domain inside the dilated body, then a volume comparison for the Minkowski sum of the lattice points with that domain.
items.proof_completeness: self-contained
known_issues_in_paper: The identity G(K) = vol((K intersect Z^n) + S) uses that the translates of S by distinct lattice points are interiorly disjoint and each has volume 1.
The paper notes that the same tiling strategy appears in the proof of Blichfeldt's classical variant of Theorem 2.1, and that convex tilings of this kind need not exist.

items.statement_informal: If the body's integer translates cover space, its number of interior lattice points is at least its volume times (1 - covering radius) to the power n.
items.statement_formal: If mu(K) <= 1 then G(int K) >= vol(K) (1 - mu(K))^n.
items.proof_as_in_paper: Apply van der Corput's Theorem 2.1 to K' = (1 - mu) int K to get t with vol(K') <= G(K' + t). Since K + Z^n = R^n one may assume t in mu K. Then vol(K)(1 - mu)^n = vol(K') <= G(K' + t) <= G((1 - mu) int K + mu K) = G(int K).

items.label: Lemma 3.2
items.name: Six properties of the Blaschke shaking

human.statement: Lemma 3.2, items i) to vi)
human.proof: Sec. 3, Proof of Lemma 3.2

background_notation.d_z: the signed Euclidean distance from u^perp to the fibre of K over z

hypotheses: For items v) and vi), u = e_i for some i in [n].
items.statement_informal: Shaking contains the projection, preserves volume, preserves the gauge in the shaking direction, does not increase the gauge of a projected point, and, when the direction is a coordinate vector, does not decrease the lattice point count nor increase the interior lattice point count.
items.statement_formal: i) K|u^perp is contained in sh_u(K); ii) vol(K) = vol(sh_u(K)); iii) |u|_cs(K) = |u|_cs(sh_u(K)); iv) |x|_cs(K) >= |(x|u^perp)|_cs(sh_u(K)) for all x in R^n; and for u = e_i, v) G(K) <= G(sh_{e_i}(K)); vi) G(int K) >= G(int sh_{e_i}(K)).
items.proof_as_in_paper: i) and ii) follow directly from the definition. For iii), writing u = (r/2)(x - y) and projecting onto u^perp gives x|u^perp = y|u^perp; with l_z = z + Ru for z in K|u^perp and d_z the signed distance from u^perp to l_z intersect K, one has d_x = d_y and z in K iff z - d_z u in sh_u(K), so from r(x-y)/2 = r((x - d_x u) - (y - d_x u))/2 one gets u in r cs(K) iff u in r cs(sh_u(K)). For iv), let r = |x|_cs(K)^{-1}; there are a, b in K with r x = (a - b)/2, and by i) r (x|u^perp) = (a|u^perp - b|u^perp)/2 lies in cs(sh_u(K)), so |r x|u^perp|_cs(sh_u(K)) <= 1. For v), the number of integer points in an interval [a,b] is maximized when a is an integer: with delta = a - floor(a), card((I - delta) intersect Z) = floor(b - delta) - ceil(a - delta) + 1 = floor(b - delta) - floor(a) + 1 >= floor(b) - floor(a) = floor(b) - ceil(a) + 1 = card(I intersect Z); the lattice points of K and of sh_{e_i}(K) lie in intervals of the same lengths, and in the shaken body those intervals start at a lattice point. vi) is the same argument with open intervals, where translating to start at a lattice point can only lose points.
items.proof_technique: Fibrewise translation, Fubini for the volume, an explicit floor and ceiling count for the one-dimensional lattice statements.
items.proof_completeness: self-contained
known_issues_in_paper: In the chain for v) the identity floor(b - delta) - ceil(a - delta) + 1 = floor(b - delta) - floor(a) + 1 holds because a - delta = floor(a) is an integer, so its ceiling is itself.
Item vi) as printed has an unbalanced parenthesis: G(int K) >= G(int(sh_{e_i}(K)).
Item ii) is stated for all u, and its proof 'follows directly from the definition'; the underlying fact is that the fibres keep their length, which is Fubini in coordinates adapted to u.

items.label: Sec. 3, first sentence of the Proof of Theorem 3.1
items.name: The paper's four functionals are invariant under unimodular transformations
items.kind_note: An asserted notation bridge used to justify the Hermite-normal-form reduction; the paper does not prove it separately.

human.statement: Sec. 3, first sentence of the Proof of Theorem 3.1

background_notation.U: a unimodular integer linear transformation of R^n

items.statement_informal: A unimodular change of coordinates preserves volume, the closed and interior lattice-point enumerators, and every successive minimum.
items.statement_formal: vol(U K) = vol(K), G(U K) = G(K), G(int(U K)) = G(int K), and lambda_i(U K) = lambda_i(K) for every i in [n].
items.proof_as_in_paper: Asserted in one sentence. The bridge expands as follows: |det U| = 1 gives volume invariance; U is a bijection of Z^n and maps interiors to interiors, giving both enumerator identities; cs(U K) = U(cs(K)), and U preserves linear independence over R, giving invariance of all successive minima.
items.proof_technique: Change of variables, the lattice automorphism U : Z^n equivalently Z^n, and transport of the central symmetral and independent lattice vectors.
items.proof_completeness: paper assertion; the catalog records every constituent that Lean must prove

items.label: Sec. 3, first sentence of the Proof of Theorem 3.1
items.name: A unimodular ambient transformation makes independent integer vectors triangular
items.kind_note: The exact consequence of Schrijver, Section 4.1, used by the paper; cataloged separately from Theorem 3.1 so the external algebraic input is not hidden in proof prose.

human.statement: Sec. 3, first sentence of the Proof of Theorem 3.1, citation to Schrijver Section 4.1

background_notation.A: the nonsingular integer matrix [v_1, ..., v_n] whose columns are the chosen vectors

hypotheses: v_1, ..., v_n are linearly independent vectors in Z^n.
items.statement_informal: One unimodular change of ambient integer coordinates sends the chosen independent vectors to the columns of an upper-triangular matrix.
items.statement_formal: There exists U in GL(n,Z) such that the matrix [U v_1, ..., U v_n] is upper triangular.
items.proof_as_in_paper: The paper cites Hermite normal form. Schrijver's Theorem 4.1 says that a rational full-row-rank matrix can be brought to [B 0], with B lower triangular, by elementary column operations. Apply it to A^T: there is a unimodular V with A^T V = B lower triangular. Transposing gives V^T A = B^T upper triangular, so U = V^T is the required unimodular ambient transformation. This transpose bridge is essential: applying column operations directly to A would replace the individual vectors and would not preserve their separately assigned gauges.
items.proof_technique: Hermite normal form applied to the transpose, then transpose the matrix identity.
items.proof_completeness: relies on external Schrijver, Theory of Linear and Integer Programming, Theorem 4.1
external_dependencies: Schrijver, Theory of Linear and Integer Programming, Section 4.1, Theorem 4.1.
known_issues_in_paper: Schrijver's convention is lower triangular and uses column operations. The paper's upper-triangular ambient-coordinate conclusion follows only after applying the theorem to the transpose, as made explicit here.

lean.route_note: Triangularization is obtained through the integer module basis machinery and realized as a real unimodular change of coordinates.

items.label: Theorem 3.1
items.name: Every convex body has an anti-blocking companion with the same volume and no worse parameters

human.statement: Theorem 3.1, items i) to iv)
human.proof: Sec. 3, Proof of Theorem 3.1, with Claims 1 and 2

items.statement_informal: For every convex body there is an anti-blocking body with the same volume, at least as many lattice points, at most as many interior lattice points, and successive minima that are no larger.
items.statement_formal: There is an anti-blocking convex body A contained in the non-negative orthant with i) vol(K) = vol(A); ii) G(K) <= G(A); iii) G(int K) >= G(int A); iv) lambda_i(K) >= lambda_i(A) for all i in [n].
items.proof_as_in_paper: Choose linearly independent v_1, ..., v_n in Z^n with |v_i|_cs(K) = lambda_i(K). All functionals involved are invariant under unimodular transformations, so one may assume the matrix [v_1, ..., v_n] upper triangular, for instance in Hermite normal form. Put K_0 = K and K_j = sh_{e_j}(K_{j-1}); the claim is that A := K_n works. Claim 1, proved by induction on j, produces at each stage independent integer vectors u_1, ..., u_n with |u_i|_{cs(K_j)} <= lambda_i(K) whose matrix is block diagonal with a j by j diagonal block and an (n-j) by (n-j) upper triangular block; the induction step replaces u_i by its projection on e_{j+1}^perp for i not equal to j+1 and uses Lemma 3.2 iv) and iii). Hence lambda_i(A) <= lambda_i(K). Properties i) to iii) follow from repeated application of Lemma 3.2 ii), v) and vi). Claim 2, again by induction, shows that x in K_j implies x|e_i^perp in K_j for all i <= j, which at j = n says that A is anti-blocking.
items.proof_technique: Successive coordinate shakings, an induction that keeps a block-triangular basis of near-minimal gauge, and a second induction for the anti-blocking property.
items.proof_completeness: self-contained given unimodular_invariance_of_paper_functionals, hermite_normal_form_adapted_basis, lemma_3_2_shaking_properties, claim_1_block_triangular_basis and claim_2_coordinate_projection_stability
known_issues_in_paper: Invariance of all four functionals under unimodular transformations is asserted rather than proved; it is what allows the reduction to a triangular basis.
The shaken bodies K_j are convex by the cited result of Campi, Colesanti and Gronchi, and compact; compactness is needed for the minima of the shaken body to be attained and is not discussed.

items.label: Claim 1
items.name: A block-triangular basis of near-minimal gauge survives each shaking

human.statement: Claim 1, with its unnumbered matrix display
human.proof: Sec. 3, paragraph following Claim 1

background_notation.K_j: the body obtained from K by shaking successively in the directions e_1, ..., e_j
background_notation.D_j: a j by j diagonal block

hypotheses: The matrix of the vectors realizing the minima of K is upper triangular.
items.statement_informal: After the first j shakings there is still an independent integer basis whose gauges are bounded by the original successive minima and whose matrix has a diagonal block on the already-shaken coordinates.
items.statement_formal: For j in {0, ..., n} there are linearly independent u_1, ..., u_n in Z^n with |u_i|_{cs(K_j)} <= lambda_i(K) whose matrix [u_1, ..., u_n] has the block form with a j by j diagonal block D_j and an (n-j) by (n-j) upper triangular block T_{n-j}.
items.proof_as_in_paper: For j = 0 take u_i = v_i. Assuming the claim for j < n, set u_i' = u_i|e_{j+1}^perp for i not equal to j+1 and u_{j+1}' = u_{j+1}. Since K_{j+1} = sh_{e_{j+1}}(K_j), Lemma 3.2 iv) and the induction hypothesis give |u_i'|_{cs(K_{j+1})} = ||u_i|e_{j+1}^perp|_{cs(K_{j+1})} <= |u_i|_{cs(K_j)} <= lambda_i(K) for i not equal to j+1, and Lemma 3.2 iii) gives |u_{j+1}'|_{cs(K_{j+1})} = |u_{j+1}|_{cs(K_j)} <= lambda_{j+1}(K). The new matrix differs from the old only by zeros in the (j+1)-th row after the diagonal entry, so the system is still linearly independent and has the required shape.
items.proof_technique: Induction on the number of shakings, projecting the basis vectors and using the two gauge properties of Lemma 3.2.
items.proof_completeness: self-contained given lemma_3_2_shaking_properties
known_issues_in_paper: The projections u_i|e_{j+1}^perp are integer vectors because the coordinates are the standard ones; this is used silently.
Linear independence after the projection is argued from the shape of the matrix, which requires the diagonal entries to remain non-zero.

items.label: Claim 2
items.name: The shaken body is closed under projection onto the already-shaken coordinate hyperplanes

human.statement: Claim 2, with Fig. 2
human.proof: Sec. 3, paragraph following Claim 2

hypotheses: K is in K^n and K_j is obtained by shaking K successively in directions e_1, ..., e_j.
items.statement_informal: After the first j shakings, projecting any point of the body onto any of the first j coordinate hyperplanes stays inside the body; at j = n this is exactly the anti-blocking property.
items.statement_formal: For j in {0, ..., n} and x in K_j, x|e_i^perp is in K_j for all 1 <= i <= j.
items.proof_as_in_paper: For j = 0 the statement is empty. Assume it for j and let x be in K_{j+1}. Lemma 3.2 i) gives x|e_{j+1}^perp in K_{j+1}. For i <= j, let x_{j+1} be the (j+1)-th entry of x and let y in K_j be the lowest point, with respect to e_{j+1}, of the fibre of K_j over x|e_{j+1}^perp. Then [y, y + x_{j+1} e_{j+1}] is contained in K_j, and by induction so is [y|e_i^perp, y|e_i^perp + x_{j+1} e_{j+1}]. Since (y|e_i^perp)|e_{j+1}^perp = (x|e_i^perp)|e_{j+1}^perp, the segment from (x|e_i^perp)|e_{j+1}^perp of length x_{j+1} in direction e_{j+1} lies in K_{j+1}, and its endpoint is x|e_i^perp.
items.proof_technique: Induction on the number of shakings, using the lowest point of a fibre and the definition of the shaking.
items.proof_completeness: self-contained given lemma_3_2_shaking_properties
external_dependencies: Campi, Colesanti and Gronchi, proof of Lemma 1.2, which the paper says this argument essentially reproduces.
known_issues_in_paper: The induction is stated for j in {0, ..., n} but the step assumes the claim 'for some j in [n]' and proves it for j+1, so the base case j = 0 and the range of the step do not line up exactly as printed.
That the segment [y|e_i^perp, y|e_i^perp + x_{j+1} e_{j+1}] lies in K_j uses the induction hypothesis applied to every point of the segment, not only to its endpoints.

items.label: Lemma 3.3
items.name: An anti-blocking body realizes its successive minima at the standard basis

human.statement: Lemma 3.3
human.proof: Sec. 3, Proof of Lemma 3.3

hypotheses: K is in K^n and anti-blocking.
items.statement_informal: For an anti-blocking body the coordinates can be permuted so that the gauge of the i-th standard basis vector is the i-th successive minimum, and then the point (2/lambda_i) e_i lies in the body.
items.statement_formal: After a permutation of coordinates, |e_i|_cs(K) = lambda_i(K) for all i, and then (2/lambda_i(K)) e_i is in K for all i.
items.proof_as_in_paper: Let v_1, ..., v_n be independent with |v_i|_cs(K) = lambda_i(K). There is a permutation sigma with the sigma_i-th entry of v_i non-zero, since otherwise the determinant of [v_1, ..., v_n] would vanish; take sigma to be the identity. Since K is anti-blocking, the projection w_i of v_i onto span{e_i} is in K, and repeated use of Lemma 3.2 iv) gives |w_i|_cs(K) <= |v_i|_cs(K) = lambda_i(K). Minimality of the minima and w_i in span{e_i} intersect Z^n force w_i = e_i and |e_i|_cs(K) = lambda_i(K). For the second part, |e_i|_cs(K) = lambda_i(K) gives (1/lambda_i(K)) e_i = (a - b)/2 for some a, b in K; since 1/lambda_i(K) is the largest r with r e_i in cs(K), the i-th coordinate of b must vanish, so b lies in e_i^perp, and anti-blocking gives (2/lambda_i(K)) e_i = ((2/lambda_i(K)) e_i + b)|span{e_i} = a|span{e_i} in K.
items.proof_technique: A permutation argument from the non-vanishing determinant, projection onto coordinate axes, and the definition of the gauge.
items.proof_completeness: gap: the stated projection membership is false and the one-line minimality argument must be replaced by a multiplicity-safe ordering argument
known_issues_in_paper: The sentence that the coordinate-axis projection w_i of v_i is contained in K is false in general: for a sufficiently small anti-blocking box, v_i = e_i realizes a successive minimum while e_i is not in K. What is true and needed is |w_i|_cs(K) <= |v_i|_cs(K), obtained directly from closure of an anti-blocking body under coordinate projections; Lemma 3.2 iv) is stated for a shaking and is not the right justification here.

The projection is initially w_i = m_i e_i for a nonzero signed integer m_i, not necessarily e_i. Gauge monotonicity gives |e_i|_cs(K) <= lambda_i/|m_i|, but for i > 1 this does not by itself invoke the defining minimality of lambda_i. One must compare the ordered gauges of all coordinate axes with the dimension thresholds, including blocks of repeated minima, and choose signs separately.
items.formalization_notes: Orient each matched lattice vector so its selected coordinate is positive, project to obtain a nonzero integer multiple of a coordinate axis, and derive an upper bound for that axis gauge. Sort the n axis gauges and use the definition of successive minima in both directions: the first i axes give lambda_i <= the i-th ordered axis gauge, while the matching bounds and a counting/order-statistics argument give the reverse inequality even across repeated-minimum blocks. Then show the positive point (2/lambda_i)e_i lies in K by the paper's extremal central-symmetral argument.

items.label: Claim 3, Eqs. (4.3), (4.4), (4.5)
items.name: The enumerator of a translate is bounded by projected enumerators over subsets of the support

human.statement: Claim 3, Eq. (4.3)
human.proof: Sec. 4, Proof of Theorem 1.3, the induction following Claim 3

background_notation.supp_B(x): the set of indices with non-zero coefficient in the expansion of x in the ordered independent set B

hypotheses: B = { b_1, ..., b_n } is a linearly independent subset of Lambda.
K is a convex bounded, not necessarily closed, subset of span(Lambda).
items.statement_informal: Translating a convex set can add at most the projected counts over the subsets of the support of the translation vector.
items.statement_formal: G_Lambda(K + t) <= sum_{I subseteq supp_B(t)} G_{Lambda|L_I^perp}(K|L_I^perp), where L_I = span{ b_i : i in I }.
items.proof_as_in_paper: For t = 0 the only summand is I empty and the inequality is a tautology. For n = 1 and non-zero t, Eq. (4.3) reads Eq. (4.4), G_Lambda(K + t) <= G_Lambda(K) + 1, which holds because a convex body in R^1 is an interval. For n > 1 the proof is by induction on the size of the support. If supp_B(t) = {1}, so t = alpha_1 b_1 with alpha_1 non-zero, then G_Lambda(K + t) = sum over x in K|b_1^perp intersect Lambda|b_1^perp of G_Lambda((K + t) intersect (x + R b_1)); the summands are segments parallel to t, so Eq. (4.4) applies and gives Eq. (4.5), G_Lambda(K + t) <= sum (G_Lambda(K intersect (x + R b_1)) + 1) = G_Lambda(K) + G_{Lambda|b_1^perp}(K|b_1^perp). For a general t, pick j in supp_B(t), set t' = t - alpha_j b_j, t'' = t'|b_j^perp, B' = B minus b_j and B'' = B'|b_j^perp, so that supp_B(t') = supp_{B''}(t'') = supp_B(t) minus j. Then G_Lambda(K + t) = G_Lambda(K + t' + alpha_j b_j) <= G_Lambda(K + t') + G_{Lambda|b_j^perp}((K + t')|b_j^perp) = G_Lambda(K + t') + G_{Lambda|b_j^perp}(K|b_j^perp + t''), and applying the induction hypothesis to both terms and recombining the two families of subsets gives the sum over all I contained in supp_B(t).
items.proof_technique: Induction on the size of the support of the translation vector, with the one-dimensional interval count as the base and a fibrewise decomposition along b_j.
items.proof_completeness: self-contained
known_issues_in_paper: The recombination step writes sum over I contained in supp(t) minus j of the two terms and identifies the second family with the subsets containing j; this uses (Lambda|b_j^perp)|L-tilde_I^perp = Lambda|L_{I union j}^perp, which is stated as an equality of enumerators without comment.

The base case is stated for n = 1 and then used inside the induction for arbitrary n on one-dimensional fibres; the fibres are segments in a translate of R b_1, so the reduction is legitimate but the quantifier over n moves.
K is allowed to be non-closed here, which is what lets the final application take K = int K.

items.label: Sec. 4, display after the Proof of Theorem 1.1
items.name: Davenport's inequality for anti-blocking bodies, by a prism decomposition

human.statement: Sec. 4, paragraph 'Since K is anti-blocking in our case, (1.10) can also be derived directly'
human.proof: Same paragraph, with its two unnumbered displays

hypotheses: K is in K^n and anti-blocking.
items.statement_informal: For an anti-blocking body Davenport's inequality follows in three lines: the lattice points thickened by a unit cube fit inside the body thickened by the same cube, and that Minkowski sum splits into disjoint prisms indexed by coordinate subsets.
items.statement_formal: G(K) = vol((K intersect Z^n) + [-1,0]^n) <= vol(K + [-1,0]^n) = sum_{k=0}^n sum_{I in binom([n],k)} vol_{n-k}(K|L_I^perp), using K + [-1,0]^n = union over I subseteq [n] of { x in R^n : x|L_I^perp in K|L_I^perp and x_i in [-1,0] for all i in I }.
items.proof_as_in_paper: The two displays: the first is the chain of equalities and the inequality; the second is the prism decomposition, which the paper says holds because K is anti-blocking.
items.proof_technique: Thickening the lattice points by a unit cube and decomposing the Minkowski sum of an anti-blocking body with the cube into disjoint prisms.
items.proof_completeness: self-contained
known_issues_in_paper: The decomposition is correctly indexed by all I subseteq [n], but the following sum is printed from k = 1. The empty-set prism is K itself and contributes vol_n(K), so the intended sum must start at k = 0; excluding the empty prism would make the displayed volume equality false.
Disjointness of the prisms is asserted; it follows from the anti-blocking property but is not argued.
items.formalization_notes: Prove the corrected k = 0 identity directly from the all-subsets prism decomposition. This is an internal proof of the anti-blocking specialization and does not depend on the separately quoted Davenport theorem.

lean.route_note: The sum includes the empty coordinate subset (the full-dimensional volume). This is the anti-blocking specialization, not the general Davenport item.

items.label: Sec. 5, Eq. (5.3)
items.name: The section length function of the reduced planar body decreases at least linearly

human.statement: Sec. 5, Eq. (5.3), inside the Proof of Theorem 1.4

background_notation.f(t): vol_1(K intersect l_t), the length of the horizontal section at height t

hypotheses: K is in K^2, anti-blocking, with |e_i|_cs(K) = lambda_i and contained in the half plane x_1 + x_2 <= 2/lambda_1.
items.statement_informal: For the reduced planar body, the length of the horizontal section at height t drops at least as fast as t.
items.statement_formal: f(t) <= f(0) - t = 2/lambda_1 - t for all t in [0, 2/lambda_2].
items.proof_as_in_paper: Immediate from the inclusion of K in the half plane x_1 + x_2 <= 2/lambda_1, together with f(0) = 2/lambda_1.
items.proof_technique: The diagonal constraint produced by the planar reduction.
items.proof_completeness: self-contained given lemma_5_1_properties_of_the_planar_reduction
known_issues_in_paper: f(0) = 2/lambda_1 uses that the reduced body meets the horizontal axis in a segment of exactly that length, which comes from Lemma 3.3 and the diagonal containment.

items.label: Lemma 5.1
items.name: Eight properties of the planar reduction under the diagonal

human.statement: Lemma 5.1, items i) to viii)
human.proof: Sec. 5, Proof of Lemma 5.1

background_notation.T: the composite shaking sh_{e_2} after sh_{-e_1, D} after sh_{-e_2, D}
background_notation.D: a lattice diagonal { x : x_1 + x_2 = m } with m an integer

hypotheses: K is in K^2, anti-blocking, with |e_i|_cs(K) = lambda_i(K).
items.statement_informal: Shaking the planar body first up against a lattice diagonal, then sideways against it, then back down, produces a body that is convex, anti-blocking, of the same volume, with no fewer lattice points, no more interior lattice points, a first minimum that has not increased, an unchanged second minimum, and which lies under the diagonal determined by its own first minimum.
items.statement_formal: A is i) convex, ii) anti-blocking, iii) of volume vol(K), iv) with G(A) >= G(K), v) with G(int A) <= G(int K), vi) with lambda_1(A) <= lambda_1(K), vii) with lambda_2(A) = lambda_2(K), and viii) contained in { x in R^2 : x_1 + x_2 <= 2/lambda_1(A) }.
items.proof_as_in_paper: i) The general shaking preserves convexity, proved through Lemma 5.3 as in shaking_preserves_convexity. ii), vi) and vii): with B = [0, 2/lambda_1(K)] x [0, 2/lambda_2(K)], one has K contained in B and by Lemma 5.3 A contained in T(B); the vertical segments of T(B) have length at most 2/lambda_2(K), while the triangle Delta = conv{0, (2/lambda_1(K)) e_1, (2/lambda_2(K)) e_2} is contained in K and satisfies T(Delta) = Delta because lambda_1(K) <= lambda_2(K), so the segment over the origin in A has length exactly 2/lambda_2(K); since A intersect e_2^perp = A|e_2^perp by construction, one gets A intersect e_1^perp = A|e_1^perp as well, so A is anti-blocking with |e_2|_cs(A) = lambda_2(K) and |e_1|_cs(A) <= |e_1|_cs(Delta) = lambda_1. iii) follows from Fubini applied in the directions span{u} and u^perp, since for any shaking sh_{u,l}(K)|u^perp = K|u^perp and the fibre lengths are unchanged. iv) and v) are proved as Lemma 3.2 v) and vi), because pi_{-e_i, D}(Z^2) = Z^2 intersect D, so every shaken lattice segment has a lattice point on D as an endpoint. viii) Let p be the lowest point of the diagonal lying in sh_{-e_1,D}(sh_{-e_2,D}(K)); then that body is contained in conv{ m e_2, p|e_1^perp, p } where m is the integer with m e_2 in D, and applying sh_{e_2} to both sides gives A contained in conv{0, (2/lambda_1(A)) e_1, (2/lambda_1(A)) e_2}, which lies in the stated half plane.
items.proof_technique: Monotonicity of the shaking under inclusion, a box and a triangle as comparison bodies, Fubini in the shaking direction, and the lattice-diagonal version of the one-dimensional counting argument.
items.proof_completeness: self-contained given lemma_5_3_shaking_is_monotone and lemma_3_2_shaking_properties
known_issues_in_paper: The value m of the lattice diagonal is said to be arbitrary because lattice translations do not change the parameters involved; the choice is fixed only implicitly.

In the proof of ii), vi) and vii), after establishing K subseteq B and hence T(K) subseteq T(B), the paper says the vertical segments of sh_{-e_1,D}(sh_{-e_2,D}(B)) are no longer than those of sh_{-e_2,D}(K). That comparison has the wrong body: monotonicity from K subseteq B points in the opposite direction. The box estimate only needs comparison with the vertical fibres of sh_{-e_2,D}(B), all of length 2/lambda_2(K).

In the proof of viii) the final containment is written with 2/lambda_1(A) on both axes, while the intermediate triangle is stated with 2/lambda_1(K) on the first axis and 2/lambda_2(K) on the second; the passage between the two uses vi) and vii).

Item iii) invokes Fubini for the oblique shaking, where the product decomposition is along span{u} and a line l not orthogonal to u; the paper removed the justifying sentence to a comment in the source.

The normalized input hypotheses are discharged for the main theorem by exists_normalized_antiBlocking and exists_planar_reduction. items.label: Lemma 5.2
items.name: Trapezoid and tangent bounds for the integral of a concave function

human.statement: Lemma 5.2
human.proof: Sec. 5, Proof of Lemma 5.2

hypotheses: For the second inequality, f is differentiable at a.
items.statement_informal: The integral of a concave function is at least the trapezoid through its endpoints and at most the integral of its tangent at the left endpoint.
items.statement_formal: (1/2)(f(a) + f(b))(b - a) <= integral_a^b f(t) dt, and if f'(a) exists, integral_a^b f(t) dt <= (b - a)(f(a) + (b - a) f'(a)/2).

items.proof_technique: Comparison with the chord and with the tangent.
items.proof_completeness: self-contained
known_issues_in_paper: The proof labels both parts 'For the upper bound'; the first paragraph proves the lower bound on the integral.
The second inequality is written with an intermediate step that is an equality for the tangent, so the displayed chain contains a redundant inequality sign.

items.label: Lemma 5.3
items.name: The general planar shaking is monotone under inclusion

human.statement: Lemma 5.3
human.proof: Sec. 5, Proof of Lemma 5.3

hypotheses: K and L are in K^2 with K contained in L.
l is a line in R^2.
u is a non-zero vector not parallel to l.
items.statement_informal: Shaking preserves inclusion.
items.statement_formal: sh_{u,l}(K) is contained in sh_{u,l}(L).
items.proof_as_in_paper: Let x be in sh_{u,l}(K). Then x is in pi(K), which is contained in pi(L), and vol_1(K intersect (x + Ru)) <= vol_1(L intersect (x + Ru)); since x lies in the segment from pi(x) of the first length, it lies in the segment of the second, which is contained in sh_{u,l}(L).
items.proof_technique: Comparing fibre lengths and the segments they generate.
items.proof_completeness: self-contained
external_dependencies: Campi, Colesanti and Gronchi, Lemma 1.1 (iii), where the paper says this is widely known for classical shakings.
known_issues_in_paper: The hypothesis is written as u in R^n minus {0} inside a planar statement; the intended space is R^2.
